utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we'll be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis with Judge Morrison away. This will continue for the remainder of this week. Good morning, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Ms. Emily Elliot, who holds degrees in politics and law from the UK, and she's been with us since last November. Thank you, kindly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. May we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Due to the protective measures granted to the witness, we'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mention this one -- seeing this one dead body, but you did see others, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't see other bodies behind that body. I assume that it was done at the time when we were absent from the Omarska camp, in other words at night.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I mean, did you -- you did see other dead bodies around the camp. We have evidence in this case that dead bodies could be seen lying around the camp, in particular near the white house, on a very regular basis. Now, you worked in the camp for almost three months, eight to ten hours every day. And is it your evidence that you didn't see at any other time during that period any dead bodies lying around the camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time I saw this one body, I didn't see any others.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about at any other -- on any other occasion, is it your evidence that you saw no other bodies on any other occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, now I can't remember exactly. Next to the white house?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Anywhere.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In your Stanisic/Zupljanin testimony, you refer to the Omarska camp a number of times as a remand centre. This wasn't a remand prison for the huge number of persons detained there, was it? A remand -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We started working there and we called it the operative investigation centre. In time, as people started arriving in large numbers, I can agree - and I concede - that it could no longer be called a reception investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's right, because a remand prison is where suspects who have been charged are held awaiting trial, and it also requires a remand order for the detention, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the case under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You either have a detention order issued by the police to hold someone for three days or a court order for 30 days which can be extended by a chamber of a court for an additional period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In normal circumstances that is the case. However, there was a state of war in Prijedor at the time. A conflict broke out between the paramilitary formations on the one hand and the police and the army on the other. Certain areas of town and villages in the municipality of Prijedor were being mopped up, and simply this could not be adhered to at this point. I do agree with you that what you've just said is the procedure under the law.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No charges were brought against the overwhelmingly vast majority of detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And some civilians were held for up to nearly three months without any justification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, in my evidence in Zupljanin and Stanisic, I said that our position was that in respect of those persons about whom there was no interesting operative information, and that was category 3 under our categorisation, should be released. However, an order arrived from Mr. Drljaca that nobody should be released regardless of the intelligence gathered about them, and that's how this group of more than 1.000 individuals stayed on in Omarska throughout the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now we have an exhibit in this case, P02772, dated the 5th of August, 1992, from the Prijedor SJB which states that 1.446 people for which valid documentation exists would be transferred to Manjaca. And on the 6th of August, 1992, over a thousand detainees were transferred from Omarska to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, I need to go into private session to continue this questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is your last topic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You testified at transcript page 16790 to 16791 that the camp was cleaned up where -- the individuals who stayed in the camp for the ICRC visit and that additional beds were brought in. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, we're going to need to go into private session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are now in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Ms. Sutherland, you conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency, a few questions. Good morning, your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would kindly like to ask for assistance if I do not say on time that we should go into closed session, but I assume that won't be necessary. I'll do my best. Please, Witness, today on page 12 you gave an answer in the affirmative to the effect that these 175 persons were left in Omarska only so that they could be shown as such to the International Red Cross. Was that the only reason why these 175 persons were left there after the transport of the other 1.000 to Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the reason I know. As for other reasons, no. Right now I haven't got any explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Beforehand, when there were several thousand there, could you have obtained these beds and could you have made it more comfortable?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. In terms of the number of people who were there, it was not possible. There wasn't enough room for all those beds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 11, a document was shown to you, D30752, and it says there that I don't know how many - 400-something - had been dealt with and a promise is being made that within a week others would be dealt with. But before that, I'd like to ask you the following: Do you know whether, and if so to what extent, the ministry and the CSB from Banja Luka made sure that these investigations were based on the law? Did they send orders, documents, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The chief of the Prijedor station, Mr. Drljaca, received all of that because they were linked to Banja Luka from an organisational point of view. I mean, Simo would from time to time give us information specifically in relation to that unit. I mean, they had come from Banja Luka to help. As for the other details, I cannot say because I was in Omarska all the time and I was not in a position to see all of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown D3968.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If the participants --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed further, could the Chamber move into private session very briefly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session. Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, please, take a look at this, the 9th of August, Drljaca is sending information to the security services centre of Banja Luka that is in charge. And look at this, it says in the second paragraph, right now -- or rather, at this moment 175 prisoners of war are at this centre and they are being processed criminally in order to establish individual responsibilities in the armed rebellion in the Prijedor municipality territory. And further on, it says that it is an open centre. You knew of one purpose. Do you allow for the possibility that this was another reason why the 175 were left there, so that investigations could be carried out fully?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know right now. I mean, really I cannot recall, I mean whether there were any additional investigations at that point in time in relation to these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 1D02954.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Witness, do you know what was the date? The 16th of August. Do you know whether all of the documents were sent to Manjaca? Full documentation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I guess so, but I cannot say anything because I no longer took part in the elaboration of that documentation; that is to say that I went to the official premises of the state security and continued work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We haven't got the original Serbian version, so I'm going to read this out to you, the part that matters. The reference is the dispatch of the 19th of August. And now I'm going to read it out in English so that they could translate this for you. [In English] "We repeat our orders that all CSBs, SJBs, and their organisational units, that is all staff of the Ministry of Internal Affairs, must treat prisoners of war and civilian refugee in a manner which is in accordance with the laws, within the competence of the MUP and compliance with the standards set by the law of war and international conventions pertinent to these matters. "You are requested to immediately report to the ministry of any existence of illicit prisoners, camps, and similar facilities, and on any persons who may have violated the laws of international conventions in their treatment of prisoners of war and refugees." [Interpretation] A moment ago you said to us that at morning meetings you cautioned people. This position of the ministry and of the CSB, how does that fit into your own experience? What was the position of the authorities on the whole, as far as the treatment of detainees and refugees was concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the position of the authorities was that people should work in accordance with the law and as stated in this dispatch, this document. However, in Prijedor, practically, something happened and the law was not observed to a large extent; that is to say, things happened, things that were not supposed to happen on the basis of the law. And I'm saying that, I mean, for the most part, this is something that individuals did, a small number of guards and a small number of inspectors. Quite simply, they did not behave in accordance with their authority or in accordance with the law. A few times I issued warnings, cautions, to guards and colleagues from Banja Luka, too. And this guard gave me the following comment: He asked me whether I felt sorry for Muslims if that is how I treated him, and this person from Banja Luka said, I have nothing to do with you, I have my chief in Banja Luka. And I respect this position taken by Minister Stanisic and what he sent, but individuals in Prijedor did not take that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you say whether this was a majority or a minority? Can you tell us whether this was the exception or the rule, these situations when the law was not observed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course it was a minority. I mean, a number of these reserve officers at the Prijedor station really behaved in a manner that was improper for a policeman. But it seems that they were not trained sufficiently, so they did not know how to behave. Unfortunately, even some inspectors behaved contrary to all conventions, Geneva Conventions, and these legal provisions adopted by our own authorities at the level of the republic and at the level of the organisational units, centres and stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did our authorities encourage or discourage this kind of behaviour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the whole I think that -- I mean, the authorities did indicate that all conduct should be based on law, but we see that not all individuals respected that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this is document from Stanisic addressed to the CSB Banja Luka, and then it circulated to all SJBs again. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You are correct, Excellency. The minister is having this document sent through the Banja Luka centre to the stations, but it has to do with all stations and centres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4255, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was 65 ter 18 -- 418. There is a Serbian version under that number, but I didn't manage to find it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the next number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 18430.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked, Mr. Witness, about the ban on releases. Were there individual releases, though, and could the fate of persons be controlled? Or what would ultimately happen to these individuals that would be taken out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm told that we have another one in different number which has an English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4255 will be substituted with 65 ter 18430.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to see that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not following this. What we are seeing now is 65 ter 18430. This is different from what we admitted as Exhibit D4255.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can -- we can look to provide the B/C/S document of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- D4255 if the Defence aren't able to locate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just, let's leave it. We leave it as D4255 as it is now and then we deal with this one. Please go on. Carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbian version of D4255 is 65 ter 18418, and I asked for 430, and I don't think that it's the same text. This one is of the 21st of August and the one a few moments ago was the 24th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please focus on the Serbian version, Mr. Witness, and could you help us with this. It says here: "In our dispatches we ... informed you of the position of the order of the Ministry of the Interior and other organs of the Republika Srpska regarding the disbanding of collection centres," and so on. The second paragraph says: "At the same time, chiefs of police stations were informed that they should arrange the transport and return of isolated persons to the municipalities and areas from which they had come in conjunction with the municipality authorities in those areas." How does this fit into your own knowledge about people being allowed to go home and having transportation organised for them? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say it is correct or incorrect because I don't know. I did not have this document, and, I mean, before I testified. I haven't been made aware of it. And I cannot say yes or no. I mean, quite simply, I don't know. I don't know of this activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But were people being allowed to go home? Were there releases? Does this document indicate that and do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we did release some people at -- however, at the very start of the work of the investigation centre was that those individuals, in respect of whom there was no interesting intelligence, should be released, and we did release them. However, there followed the order by Chief Drljaca that -- without consulting him. And so in the end, category 3 was sent to Trnopolje, despite our insistence that they be released; whereas the remainder were sent to Manjaca, and that's what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please look at paragraph 3. It says here: "However" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think now I understood it. The first page of the B/C/S that we are seeing now, isn't that the original version of the English that we saw as being Exhibit D4255? Because this is dated as 21st of August, but English translation is 24th of August, which is the translation of the second page of this document. I checked this reference number. I think it matches with the previous one. Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm a tad confused as well, but we can see that this document is signed by Zupljanin in the -- the original. So I'm -- and -- and the English has Drljaca's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, yes, Drljaca appears on the second page of this document. So we do not have -- that means that we do not have English translation for this first page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible, because page 2 was translated. It's page 2 in Serbian and 1 in English. It's possible, however, that this is the case. We'll look into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- is it not possible the same document signed by Mico Stanisic was circulated by Zupljanin from the CSB in Banja --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's -- that's what I'm assuming --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: -- when I'm looking at the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So we are looking at the same document, actually. But I'm not sure. So I leave it to you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, it just appears that these two documents aren't correlating at all. I mean, if we look at the first paragraph of the B/C/S, it refers to two broad numbers -- broadge [phoen] numbers and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's evident. It's obvious that the English document dated 24th is not the translation of this. That's obvious. But my question for Mr. Karadzic is whether this document is the one we already saw earlier on. But please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Elements are being repeated. This has to do with the implementation of an order or a telegram from the Ministry of the Interior at various levels, from security services centres to public security stations. Certain elements are being repeated but not everything is the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you help us? It reads: "There are some indications that isolated individuals could be subject to assault, or, rather, threats upon their return." To the best of your knowledge, who would assault them or expose them to threats upon their return? Would it be representatives of the authority or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course they would be individuals or groups holding opposite views or being members of other ethnicities and religions. That could be expected because it was a multiethnic community and such tensions were there before, and unfortunately are still present now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This position about providing protection to the released, how does it stand in relation to the position of the authorities with regard to treating these individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, based on the documents shown to me, the authorities have shown to be in favour of complying with the law, the minister of the interior sending this letter. That's to say, in my own work I always advocated the position that the individuals who did not engage in unlawful activity and in respect of whom there is no interesting intelligence should be released and be free to go about their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll mark the first page of this document for identification pending English translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4256, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, Witness, you told us that there were individual cases of people being released on occasion and that Drljaca forbade people from being released without him knowing about it. Was it the case that he banned this on condition that he be informed or that he banned it in general?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, it was about him asking that nobody should be released from the investigation centre unless he was informed about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was Mr. Drljaca a member of the Crisis Staff by virtue of his office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That should have been case.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be briefly shown P2741, which the Prosecution cited. Can we direct our attention to item 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says: "Following the appropriate procedure on the part of the competent organs, the other prisoners found to be innocent would be released from detention." So how does this accord with your experience about this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, this accords with what I said, that we had the intention of releasing such individuals, according them freedom of movement. And that was our position from the very start, from the early days of the investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I direct your attention to the heading. It is a document of the Crisis Staff dated 2nd of June, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At page 11, we have D03752. A promise is made -- this is the 16th of August. A promise is made that the rest of the documentation will be sent in a week's time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown D1866. That date was the 17th, and now this is the 23rd of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It reads: "We are hereby informing you that documentation is required concerning the prisoners of war who have been transferred from the Omarska investigation centre" -- or rather, "that the required documentation concerning the prisoners of war who had been transferred from the Omarska investigation centre to the Manjaca prisoner of war camp was forwarded to the commander ..." So was the promise made on the 17th made good on, and was the delay deliberate or was, indeed, some time required for the documentation to be transferred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that because of the volume of documentation, the processing did take some time, hence the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question: At page 9, you were told that it was observed in Manjaca that among the prisoners there were those who were unfit to hold a rifle, let alone run. You were asked about category 2. Can you tell us, was it possible for those who were unfit to hold a rifle to commit criminal offences against general security and safety, the state, and the constitution? I'm referring to the individuals from category 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know of one case and I know the person myself. He was taken in, even though he was more than 65 years old. He had two hand-grenades that he got from a relative and that was the reason why he was brought in. I don't know of any other cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. While the witnesses here with us, the Chamber wishes to return to the issue raised yesterday in relation to the admission of 1D9645, 1D9646, 1D9647, and 1D9649, discussed during the testimony of this witness. These four documents are Official Notes or compilations thereof from 1992. The Chamber has reviewed the examples referred to by the Prosecution yesterday and wishes to remind the parties of its oral ruling of the 11th of December, 2012, in which it clarified the Chamber's position on the admission of third party statements. The Chamber noted that third party statements produced for the purpose of current criminal proceedings may only be admitted pursuant to the modalities of Rule 92 bis, 92 quater, and 92 quinquies and that in relation to any other third party statement not prepared for the purpose of current criminal proceedings, they may only be admitted if they are comment upon, confirmed, or adopted by the witness on the stand. The Chamber made further application of this ruling on the 13th of March, 2013, in relation to 65 ter 1D7846 and 65 ter 1D855. The four documents discussed yesterday fall into the category of documents not prepared for the purpose of criminal proceedings and may, therefore, be admitted if they are sufficiently comment upon, confirmed, or adopted by the witness on the stand. The Chamber is of the view that 1D9646 and 1D9647 have not been sufficiently commented by the witness in the previous proceedings for the purpose of admission. However, the Chamber considers that the witness's comments on 1D9645 and 1D9649 are sufficient for the purpose of admission of these type of documents as associated exhibits. We'll assign exhibit numbers for the last two documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 1D9649 will be Exhibit D4257. And 1D9645 will be Exhibit D4258.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Witness. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. Now you are free to go. Given the timing, the Chamber will take a break now. You will rise all together with us. We'll break for half an hour and resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you requested six hours for the cross-examination of Witness Mico Stanisic. But before that, I was wondering whether this witness should be led live in light of our practice? Mr. Stanisic refused to testify voluntarily and was therefore subpoenaed. The important witnesses in a similar situation were ordered to testify viva voce, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, there have been instances where -- where these witnesses have been -- have been ordered to testify viva voce, particularly if they were close to Dr. Karadzic. In this case, Mr. Stanisic co-operated with us and I worked with him personally to try to make what I thought was a very clear, cogent statement. And we believed that it would be better if that statement were used as a 92 ter. And given the amount of time that the Prosecution has asked for cross-examination, they should have plenty of opportunity to decide on his credibility without having to have us lead him live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given his position and the proximity with the accused, it would be consistent the Chamber should order him to testify viva voce. Mr. Tieger, do you have any observation on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. And I was scouring my memory to recall if any failure on the Prosecution's part to make a motion similar to ones it did in the past was the result of inertia or a sense that the Trial Chamber would intervene on its own or desire not to raise the issue on too many individual occasions. Nevertheless, I -- I can't identify at the moment a distinction between the witnesses for whom viva voce testimony was required based on their positions at the time and Mr. Stanisic and his position. But I did send an e-mail to see if there was something in particular that I might be missing. In any event, I think the Court's point appears to be well taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could add one more thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, can you also take into consideration that this is very late in the day, both in terms of proximity to the time of his testimony and to the close of our case. So, first of all, we invested a lot of time in preparing this statement which we wouldn't have done if we'd known that he was to be viva voce. But, more importantly, between now and the end of the case, we are trying very much to use every available moment to help prepare Dr. Karadzic's testimony. And to now have to have him prepare to lead Mr. Stanisic live will take away from that and make us less ready to begin his testimony when that time comes, which is rapidly approaching. So I hope you can take that into consideration as well. Again, I think this is a very clear, focused statement by this witness and you would not be losing anything by having his testimony under 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, since we're engaged in this discussion, simply to note that I'm not sure that necessarily follows. It would appear that the time that Mr. Robinson is referring to that was, according to him, invested in the preparation of the statement, is a -- lays the groundwork for either the submission of that statement, or, as the Court is now indicating, would be more beneficial to the Court leading the witness live. I mean, it appears that the prep work has essentially been done one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will consider this issue and will give its ruling during the course of today or first thing tomorrow. Yes. Shall we bring in the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, while we're doing that, I've been asked to advise you that we do now have the translation of Exhibit D4255 in e-court under 65 ter number 18418. And we would ask that the status of that exhibit be confirmed as a full exhibit as opposed to MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are we talking about 4255 or 4256?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We admitted in full because we had English only. So you found the original?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We found the B/C/S, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll supplement it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Do you hear me in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Will you make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jaksic. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Like with anyone who speaks our language, I have to ask you to leave a short pause between questions and answers and to speak slowly so that everything is properly recorded.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have given them a statement and signed it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D49063 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see before you that statement? I will explain these blanks. Is this the first page of the statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do not be confused by the fact that several paragraphs are blacked out. The Chamber found them to be of no assistance because they are related to events in Croatia, not Bosnia. Have you signed this statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the last page be shown, please, so that the witness may identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this statement faithfully and accurately reflect what you have said to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Completely faithfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put to you the same questions that were asked when the statement was taken, would your answers be essentially the same as in the statement?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I would not change the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement under Rule 92 ter, with the accompanying documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll deal with associated exhibit separately. Mr. Zec, do you have any objection to the admission of this statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4259, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we come to the exhibits? Mr. Robinson, if you could assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, we are offering nine associated exhibits; eight to be admitted and one to be marked for identification as it's an intercept not involving this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you are not tendering 1D7073 which has been already admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We already informed the Defence that we'll be objecting to admission to six of the exhibits because we believe they don't consist -- they don't form part -- indispensable and inseparable part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you identify the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So 1D07072 through 1 -- next is 1D07074 through 1D07077. And 65 ter 051 -- 414. The last one should be 65 ter 05414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We agree with you as regards 1D7072, 1D7074, and 1D7077. However, the Chamber is of the view as regards the remaining three - i.e., 1D7075, 7076, and 65 ter 5414 - that they satisfy the requirements for associated exhibit. But with respect to the last one, 65 ter 5414, we'll admit only those pages referred to in the statement. So we'll receive the remaining four documents and we'll mark it for identification pending the authentication, I mean, the intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the intercept we'll mark for identification is 30514. The exhibit numbers will be given in due course by the Registrar in writing. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to lead one of these documents live, one of those that were not covered by the statement by the live evidence. And now I would like, first of all, to read a short summary of Mr. Dusko Jaksic's statement. [In English] Dusko Jaksic was born on 7th of June, 1935, in Celinac, Republika Srpska. From 1992 to 1995, Dusko Jaksic was the director of the Institute of Economics in Banja Luka, also known as EIBL. He was also an assemblyman of the socialist party SDP in the Municipal Assembly of Banja Luka. In 2009, Dusko Jaksic became a senator for the Republika Srpska and was later appointed as an advisor in 2011. Issue arose as Banja Luka could not influence its own development or that of its surrounding area. This was due to the centralisation of all funds, financial institutions, and capital in Sarajevo. Banja Luka and East Bosnia and Herzegovina were therefore economically behind compared to the Sarajevo-Zenica region. Dusko Jaksic frequently tried to prove how disastrous this policy was. Dusko Jaksic advocated that Krajina be an independent state should Yugoslavia separate. A draft statute was created by Dusko Jaksic and Predrag Radic, the mayor of Banja Luka, to this effect. In addition, a document outlining the regional organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the creation of a north-west Krajina region was also drafted. Despite many people disagreeing and the constant obstruction by the Sarajevo politics, a prominent Muslim leader like Mr. Osman Karabegovic gave absolute support to Dusko Jaksic's proposals. The creation of region was not intended to breakup Bosnia and Herzegovina but instead strengthen it and set an example for Yugoslavia. Around June 1991, Dusko Jaksic and Milorad Zivanovic drafted and proclaimed the constitution of the Republic of Krajina. This constitution was signed at a meeting in Banski Dvor in Banja Luka. Due to the rumours that Krajina would be used for political bargaining and fears that this would lead to an exodus of the population, Dusko Jaksic went to Belgrade to inform Slobodan Milosevic of their concerns. Upon his arrival, Dusko Jaksic met Dr. Radovan Karadzic. Radovan Karadzic's lack of curiosity regarding Dusko Jaksic's arrival in Belgrade illustrated the two Serbian political currents and the tense relations between Republika Srpska and Krajina leadership. At the beginning of the war in 1992, Krajina lost contact with the rest of Republika Srpska in BH. And that will be short summary of his statement. Now I would like to pose a few questions to Professor Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, can you tell us how other ethnic communities in Banja Luka viewed the centralisation of funds and especially this decision contained in the document 1D7077 when you asked for these funds to remain in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: All the way up to the referendum of the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, all ethnic communities and all structures and academic circles were absolutely unanimous that a higher degree of independence and autonomy of Krajina is necessary. The processes that took place between the 1980s and 1990s were total, so all the companies in Krajina were just branch offices of companies that had headquarters in Sarajevo. In that sense, there was no disagreement between Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. The director was a Croat and he supported me absolutely, not only as somebody who had more academic experience but he supported me in a broader sense in my efforts to achieve that higher degree of independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to speak more slowly because we will have problems. Already we are missing one thing. You said that centralisation favoured central companies in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I'll give you one example. In 1969 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Banja Luka experienced an earthquake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just is a second, Mr. Jaksic. If you want to say something after Mr. Karadzic's words, please give us some pause because both Mr. Karadzic's words and your words have to be translated. Yes, could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One example, in 1960 [as interpreted], the city of Banja Luka experienced a destructive earthquake, seven degrees by Richter. At the level of Yugoslavia, a major fund was created to reconstruct Banja Luka. That fund was not located in Banja Luka as an institution, it was based in Sarajevo, and the administration of Banja Luka and the broader area that was affected could not make any decisions for the purposeful use of these funds. From that moment on, the centralisation of all the other types in the economy and the public sector was only accelerated. There remained only one bank, the Privredna banka of Sarajevo with its branch offices in the republic. All the major companies, industrial enterprises, were based in Sarajevo, and all the way up to 1975, the only university was in Sarajevo. I wouldn't go into much detail, but the consequence of that is that Krajina began to be drained demographically very quickly, and the same goes for the eastern Bosnia as a whole. There was one form of economic association, that was the chamber of commerce. In Banja Luka, the chamber of commerce covered 17 municipalities, 16 municipalities had a lower than replacement birthrate, and only one municipality had a positive birthrate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was said about Banja Luka that it had only a symbolically positive birthrate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Witness confirms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D7077 is the document I would now like to call up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at this. This is a short record from the 13th session of the Assembly of Banja Luka municipality held on 27 November 1991, which was just two or three months before the war broke out. On the first page, Professor, is it the case that we see that it was a joint session, a session of the joint assembly, representing all ethnic communities and all parties?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There were 99 people present.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we show page 9 in Serbian and page 15 in English, and then we will look at page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Help us here, Professor, with the conclusions. Many people took part in the debate including Muslims. You were a representative of the socialist party; Ganic represented the SDA; Turkanovic [phoen] SDA; Mormerovic [phoen] SDA, and so on. Look at conclusion number 3. It deals with the preparation of a proposal to suspend allocation of funds from Banja Luka municipality for the activities at the level of the republic enumerated above and instead keep those funds in Banja Luka. Was this justified economically, and who voted in favour of this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I cannot describe the climate that prevailed at the time, but what I do know is that there was no resistance to such a conclusion being adopted along the ethnic lines. I have to emphasise that a year or a year and a half prior to this, the only bank in Bosnia-Herzegovina which detached itself from the system of banks in Sarajevo covering all the banks in Bosnia was Privredna banka Banja Luka, which got detached from Privredna banka Sarajevo. So in Bosnia we had the Privredna banka Sarajevo which had its branch offices in 108 municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina; whereas only Banja Luka had its own Privredna banka with a Croat as its CEO. And that was the start of this process of resistance to the centralisation of Sarajevo. And this is just a similar example to one that I've given about the bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this a detachment of the bank economically motivated or ethnically motivated?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I did say that the director was a Croat, Goran Pegan [phoen], and he was the one who was the greatest of advocates for this decentralisation. He had great political opponents, but I think that the Serbs were among the majority of his supporters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It reads here that the report was unanimously adopted. Was this indeed the case, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say with any certainty whether it was unanimously adopted, though I have no reason to doubt the veracity of the minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the tender the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Zec?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The witness didn't confirm anything. And secondly, I don't see relevance. But I leave it to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we now have a basis to admit it. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4260, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another question or just one more question, Professor. What was the position and what was the professional and political view of your colleagues from the international community with regard to the process of regionalisation in Bosnia-Herzegovina prior to and especially after the Dayton, if you know what these positions were?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: If I may, I would like to make two points about the events in the former state. Just as all the other eastern countries, Yugoslavia started the process of transition in terms of its political and economic systems. The transition had three pillars: The first pillar was the introduction of a multiparty system and parliamentary democracy; the second pillar was the privatisation of the state capital, i.e., companies; and the third pillar was the decentralisation and the strengthening of the role of the local government with a special emphasis on regionalisation. Six agencies were set up at the level of Yugoslavia in the respect of the six republics which were supposed to implement the transition process. Five agencies were based in five capitals of the republics. It was only in Bosnia-Herzegovina that the agency was not based in Sarajevo but rather in Banja Luka. It was entrusted with the Institute of Economics in Banja Luka and I was its director. This was during Rade Markovic's government, and the decision was made to base the agency not in Sarajevo but with the institute in Banja Luka because the feeling was that Sarajevo was not ready to carry out this task because the Sarajevo institutions and agencies would not support it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: There is one more detail, if I may. Why was this entrusted with the institute? This was the only institute in the former Yugoslavia which affirmed itself and gained a high reputation and was not based in a capital of a republic. It was often cited as a role model for other agencies which should likewise get developed without being under the influence of central republican authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us was this before the multiparty elections?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, the transition process began in 1989. We got this status in 1990. I think it coincided with the beginning of the election campaign or just before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In what way did the authorities in Sarajevo reform themselves in this process of decentralisation, or did they remain as rigid as they were before?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, these authorities tried and managed, not at the very start but later on, to halt the transition process or to slow it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And after the war, your colleagues from your profession and your international colleagues, did they have any specific suggestions to make as to how this should be done and did they accord with your own views?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: We had a project of the reconstruction of Bosnia-Herzegovina covering the period between 1996 and 2002. According to the official documentation, it involved the sum of some 5.5 billion dollars. Numerous projects were implemented covering refugees all the way to privatisation according to a new model. Between 2003 and 2005 the European commission engaged two institutions, one from Northern Ireland and another from Italy, to develop a project which aimed at setting up the regional organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina with an emphasis on economic regions. However, the latter was supposed to be designed in such a way as not to in any way impair the entities of the federation and Republika Srpska. And this sort of approach had the undivided support of the representatives of the federation, particularly the Bosniak side, but it was rejected by Republika Srpska despite the fact that to a large degree over 90 per cent the project would have created the regions in the same way as we had suggested that it be done in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 1D49064 be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this, Professor, had your proposal for the regionalisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and ours been accepted before the referendum in Bosnia-Herzegovina, how would the situation have unfolded? Would there have been a war?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was called here in the capacity of a witness, and I accepted that role for several reasons, as a fact witness. However, if I were to look at the documents and the various situations which I thought were important enough for me to appear before this Court, then I would have to mention the regionalisation project and everything that was happening around it, and I don't think it will be a waste of time if I mention the last session of the Bosnia-Herzegovina Assembly. There is one document, and I have it here, about it. The session lasted late into the night until 1.30 in the morning. This was a document entitled: "Conditions and Possibilities for the Introduction of a Regional Structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Creating the Region of North-western Bosnia, Project and Tasks," which was drafted by the Institute of Economics. So this was a project which had yet to be developed by someone. The date is March 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what it is that we are looking at on our screens?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: What we see on the screen is the front page of the document that I've mentioned. We see the title of the project -- on the right-hand side, we see the title of the project which was produced in 2004 by those two agencies that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The title is the same: Regional strategy of the regional development of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I'm referring to the title of the project that was commissioned by the European commission; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's called the EURED project. You can see the original logo here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what this map represents?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: It represents a proposal of dividing Bosnia-Herzegovina into five regions. One of them is Krajina, and that's the left-hand side of the map. It's, in fact, north-western Bosnia. And the only difference between this project and our initial project is in the municipality of Teslic, which here is added to the Central Bosnia region; whereas, we thought it should be part of the Krajina. Therefore, the scope of this region is the same except for Teslic. The remainder was supposed to be four regions, whereas in our initial document we envisaged three rather than four regions. The institute and I, myself, are very well familiar with the process of creating regions normally applied in the European Union, and everything we did was, in fact, in compliance with the standards of the European Union.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us this: Did the SDS or the political circles in general interfere with what you were doing, trying to exert some sort of pressure, or was this done solely according to the economic principles?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, this was done in 1989, 1990, when the general public was not informed of this at all -- or rather, the professional circles were very familiar with these efforts at regionalisation. Now, with the arrival of the SDS and other parties on to the scene, the already-existing climate was seized upon because it was a good basis for organising the economy in quite concrete terms in what were time of confusion, in fact. Let me repeat: Had we not been as prepared as we were and had there not been this view been taken in respect of the regions, had this preparatory work not been done, I wonder what life and the economy would have been like had the war broken out without all this having been done previously. Many professional and economic circles joined these efforts because they thought that regions, per se, were a justified form of economic organisation. Had this not been the case, other less competent individuals and institutions would have come to the fore and the situation would have been far worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In line 16 and 17, can this be corrected? The witness said: It was done in 1989, 1990, and it was general knowledge and very much known to the public rather than: It was not known. And this was at a time when the SDS was not formed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: The Institute of Economics in Sarajevo, one of the two such institutes in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the period between 1986 and 1990 implemented eight projects which had to do with the regionalisation which had been given by the scientific fund which I headed for a while. You have them in this material. They were all listed there according to the various topics that they covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I think I have to clarify this with you, Mr. Jaksic. It's about our transcript, whether it's recorded correctly. To the question of Mr. Karadzic whether SDS or the political circles in general interfere with what you were doing, trying to exert some sort of pressure, or was this done solely according to the economic principles. Your answer was recorded like this, I quote: "Well, this was done in 1989, 1990, when the general public was not informed of this at all. Or rather, the professional circles were very familiar with --"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the contrary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- "these ..." So did you say that the general public was informed of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the general public was well informed, very well informed, as a matter of fact. And that had to do with regionalisation until 1990 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a member of the SDP and I was a member of parliament for the SDP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's sufficient for your answer. Shall we mark it, this document for identification. Mr. Zec, do you have any observation or objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Again, it's about relevance but I'll leave it to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's related to the regionalisation issued in one way or another, so, as such, it may be relevant to a certain extent. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one. In line 11, it was not recorded that the witness said that the SDS did not have anything to do with regionalisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I have no further questions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in its most part in writing; that is, through your written witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now you will be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, you told us in your statement about your political background. Can you confirm that you have never been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was never a member of the SDS. I did not attend a single SDS meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you were not privy to internal SDS communications, that's also correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: A few colleagues of mine from school, from high school, that will be of great interest to you. Dr. Nikola Koljevic and I went to the same high school together for eight years. We're the same year, the same generation. Dr. Milovan Milovanovic, who was vice-president of the Assembly SDS, also went to the same class with me for eight years. Dr. Bozo Bojanic, who is a lawyer, one of the founders of the SDS in Banja Luka, is also my year. So for a man who lived in Banja Luka from elementary school until the end of high school and started university, you could not expect such a person not to have been in contact with persons who belonged to the SDS. However, these were just informal contacts and of course certain discussions that were inevitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in paragraph 16 through 27, you talk about the union of Bosanska Krajina municipalities. When this was created back in April 1991, Mr. Jaksic, other political parties - mainly, HDZ and SDA - were against this regional body because they saw it as an entity which was dominated by one ethnic group; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: That is right. That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: The -- it was established after the recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina and then the SDS, and not only the SDS, but the entire population, took advantage of what had been done in terms of regionalisation; that is to say, it was turned into this community of municipalities. And all of these --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at one article at that time and then I'll ask you more.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 25939.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is an article from "Oslobodjenje" from April 1991, which talks about the creation of the union assembly of the Bosnia Krajina municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: At English e-court page 7, and in the B/C/S it's toward the end of the page on the left side.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: There are comments made by Stjepan Kljuic from the HDZ, and he said: "What has been created, in short, is unconstitutional and I'm sure it will not be able to exist." And below that, Muhamed Cengic from SDA said: "This was done behind the backs of others." He said: "Obviously they are trying to create a state within a state." And then he continues: "Economic reasons for the association are a long way from the truth. These are primarily political reasons with a goal of creating a state for only one nation." So, Mr. Jaksic, this was the position of other political parties with respect to the union of Bosanska Krajina municipalities - right? - at the time?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: That is quite right. At that time that was quite right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6615, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, the idea of the Krajina region, or the ARK as it was called later on, was something that SDS planned and implemented; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think that that statement is right. The SDS only accepted the results and what had been achieved over two or three years before that in terms of creating a territorial form as we had envisaged the Krajina region. They had received a good basis for organisation. Of course, after the recognition of Bosnia as an independent state, that was an attempt made by the SDS to remain in Yugoslavia and to separate in that way. All of us from the regions supported that because we thought that by establishing a region with certain elements of statehood, we would have a chance of remaining in Yugoslavia. So that was not the first objective for us to get a state of Krajina. Rather, to get a Krajina - I'm talking about Krajina now - in order to remain in Yugoslavia in that way. Had we known that there would have been no Yugoslavia, then our --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: This Chamber has received evidence regarding this issue. Mr. Karadzic acknowledged that the idea of regionalisation originated from him and the SDS. This is in P2556 and P6243, English page 25, B/C/S e-court page 29. Mr. Kupresanin said at the 20th Assembly that the purpose of the region of Krajina was to destroy Alija's state. This is in D456, English page 70, B/C/S e-court page 76. So, Mr. Jaksic, the fact is that the idea of the Krajina region was something that the SDS planned and implemented; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: That's certainly not right. That's not right. Mr. Kupresanin, whom I had not known until then, and the others, used all of the materials of the economic institute, and they invited us - they invited us - to interpret that, what a region means, what that means, what it is economically, politically, so they used that to a large degree. They are founders. They are the ones who implemented that in terms of establishing bodies. However, as initiators in terms of creating this form, they had inherited something that was alive before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraphs 18, 34, 35, and 36, you talk about your idea of creating a Krajina state as a separate unit of Yugoslavia. This idea, Mr. Jaksic, was something that SDS did not like and did not want to happen. From this moment, the SDS saw you and the others who were behind this idea as someone who wanted to separate, to separate Krajina from other Serb areas and jeopardise the unity of Serbian people; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: There were major differences. However, you have to know that the Krajina was isolated for a while, totally isolated from Yugoslavia, the eastern part of Bosnia, too. We who lived there and who had strong links with the Serbs in the Krajina and Croatia, we had a large number of refugees in our area from Croatia. And isolated in such a way, we saw as our only solution -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I understand you want to explain why you were behind this idea, but my question was that the SDS was against the idea that you were about to explain; that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: The SDS was not -- of course, they were against these two lines that existed. We did not negate Republika Srpska at the time. However, on the condition -- I mean, if it would not manage to remain in Yugoslavia, then we wanted to secure for ourselves a position which would mean that we would stay in Yugoslavia. How do I put this? Politically, we were rather passive. We did not interfere in military affairs. We did not meddle in any way. We simply tried to organise the life of people there. There was a division among people but it was not very pronounced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter 25410.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is an article of an interview that you gave in 1992. And the article was published in a newspaper called "Lider." I would like you to look at the page --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Maybe we also can have a look at the second page for the witness to just recognise the -- see the articles and acknowledge that that's his interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So at the top it says -- it has your name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Second page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your -- your photo is there. Do you remember this article -- this interview?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I remember that interview. I have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we go to English page 2. In B/C/S, it should be middle of the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So here on this page, you -- that -- it's recorded, the act of creation and proclamation of the Krajina state was exclusively seen as a separatist act for which Bosanska Krajina would be separated from the rest of the Serb ethnic areas in Bosnia named republic of Serbian people in BiH which would, according to the Sarajevo SDS, jeopardise the unit of the Serbian people in this republic. And there is also a reference to the ARK Assembly of 29th February 1992, which is P5452 in this case, during which the idea of the Krajina state was denied and rejected and the RS laws imposed. So, Mr. Jaksic, the fact is that the SDS blocked your idea of the Krajina state because it was against their plans of having Serb state in Bosnia which would encompass all territories claimed as ethnic Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: That is correct. That was that attempt of ours to establish this autonomous region of the Krajina that was blocked by the SDS. However, the team that worked on this did not have any organised bodies; that is to say, there was no assembly, there were no committees. This was a gathering of intellectuals working on that. And through our actions, we wished to reinforce a belief, politically, and to make sure that the Krajina would not be involved in any trade-offs. You know that there were a countless numbers of variants of the division of Bosnia. Sorry, I know I'm speaking very fast. There were many maps that were drawn and a separation line often went through the Krajina, and it was not only with the SDS but also with the army that we presented these ultimatums saying that they could not trade with the Krajina or, rather, not have the Krajina involved in any trade-offs. And we tried to create institutions and certain documents. I'm going to tell you something now. These --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's keep a little bit longer on this topic of Krajina state, because your idea of the Krajina state was discussed at the SDS deputies club meeting on 28 February 1992, during which many comments were made about you, about Predrag Lazarevic, and about your idea of the Krajina state.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If we can have P00938.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you that we stay with this, if possible. Can we stay with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Wait for my question, please. I'm going to show you now what was said during this SDS meeting in February 1992 about --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- this same idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before we leave this document, we would ask that it be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think he will come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I am finished with this exhibit and we can admit. I didn't offer. I thought it's too long. And witness confirmed what I said, but we can admit it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long was it, then? It disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The article was, as I remember, in English 12 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we admit the first page in B/C/S and the first and second page in English. And, if necessary, other parts can be added depending upon the re-examination. Yes, shall we assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6616, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have English page 34, B/C/S e-court page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jaksic, this is what SDS thought about your idea of the Krajina state. Here is Mr. Karadzic speaking. He said: "Those Lazarevic fellows, those stuffed peacocks to whom we have made no promises because one can't promise them anything, those people to whom we have opened doors, those communists who were serfs in 1945 and participated in the efforts to make Krajina and Banja Luka poor, now they are creeping out of some institutes and trying to be a power above the government. "The Serbian Democratic Party is in power there!" So this was the view of Mr. Karadzic with respect to you, Mr. Lazarevic, and your idea of the Krajina state; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I'm going to answer and this really can explain a lot in this case. You see, the SDS won the elections in the Krajina. Most of the Serbs there voted for the SDS because they were the most numerous there. When Republika Srpska was created, the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the leadership of the SDS had to leave Sarajevo and go to Pale. A great intellectual elite of Sarajevo left Sarajevo with them and went to Pale. This is very important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can I clarify, when you say they left to Pale, what period are you talking about? We are here talking about February 1992.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: This does have to do with February and also what happened beforehand in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Both speakers are speaking at the same time so it's impossible to interpret into any language.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'm sorry for interrupting you. I'm trying to keep some way that we can follow your evidence. So we won't go now to period of war and later. Let's keep with this. Let's talk about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have an objection regarding the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Sir, did you complete your answer with respect to this part of Mr. Karadzic's intervention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not. Please, I would like to say a very important thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, if you could speak very slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can. In Banja Luka, leading intellectuals, artists, they all the remained in Banja Luka during the war and after the war. Had they been compelled to leave Banja Luka to go to a smaller place in the Krajina, that would be Knezevo, for example, that is what Pale is to Sarajevo. This movement would have been a lot more compact in the Krajina than it actually had been. This elite that is mentioned by Dr. Karadzic in this transcript, this Banja Luka elite, along with the epithets that you referred to, is equally patriotic but it was not politically organised. And they strove only to preserve the population in the Krajina. That's the only thing that they had in mind. The policy of the SDS was a lot more complex and in a far bigger territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I leave it to you Mr. Zec. Mr. Zec wanted to remind you that this was in February 1992. Please continue, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 18, it was not recorded. The witness was interrupted when he said that a great Serb intellectual elite left Sarajevo and went to Pale. That explains the rest of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I think it can be read that way as it is now. But let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.
