utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12, you discuss the influence of Serb leaders on the Bosnian Krajina. You say that Jovan Raskovic gave the SDS in Krajina stronger foundations than Karadzic. Are you saying that Mr. Raskovic was more influential than Karadzic in the SDS in the Bosnian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I cannot -- well, I think that at first, yes. At first, yes. But that went on for a little while, and then after 1991 Professor Raskovic withdrew and then the role of the SDS was dominant with the team that was in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's have a look at 65 ter 11996, which is an article from January 1991. I'm sorry, the article is from January 1992. At English page 2; B/C/S should be the third column. In the B/C/S, it's third column from second line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is what Jovan Raskovic said: "All this can sound some kind of profanity, but I believe that there is no fear of Bosnian sovereignty for the Serbian people in BiH. It would not be a genocide. I talked about that with Karadzic. He's not inclined to accept my opinion" --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please. Could the Prosecutor not skip anything once he starts reading. Now that he did start, he should read everything out. I mean, it is unfair to skip two sentences that explain everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But if you -- first, could you help me find the passage on this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So it starts with -- towards the upper part of the page, "... that true politics has not been established ..." That's in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I skipped that part and I said: "All this can sound some kind of profanity, but, believe me, there is no fear of Bosnian sovereignty for the Serbian people in BiH. This would not be genocide." Then I will skip two lines: "I talked about that with Karadzic. He's not inclined to accept my opinion. He thinks it is necessary to react in a different way if the Bosnian sovereignty is formed. According to him, the Serbs must adopt different political stand and a diverse political procedure in that case, even though it seems to me that it pushes people into a war. He has an excuse so far as to say that they caused it and we are only reacting to it. However, his reaction is without a doubt pro-war one."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So here, Mr. Jaksic, they talk about the issue of Bosnian independence. And as we see, Mr. Raskovic was not against Bosnian independence, but Mr. Karadzic insisted that Bosnian Serbs should react against it even if, as Mr. Raskovic says, it pushes people into a war. So it is not correct that Raskovic was more influential in the Bosnian Krajina than Karadzic. In fact, it was Karadzic and his influence which ultimately prevailed in the Bosnian Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did prevail, but Raskovic gave numerous statements. I don't want to cite them here, you probably know them, about both the Serbs and the war. He acted more like a free-thinking lecturer. As far as the population in Krajina is concerned, there was no distinction. According to Karadzic or to Raskovic, people believed it's absolutely the same policy. So we did not feel any conflict, nor were there any factions between Karadzic and Raskovic in Krajina. But what matters is that people with whom I worked had very little contact with Raskovic. In fact, we had no contact with him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: But you confirm this is Jovan Raskovic that you talk about and the extent to which his views were followed in Bosanska Krajina? This is the same person; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. That question, whether this is the same Jovan Raskovic is not -- I don't believe it's going -- it's a relevant question because it won't make any difference to the admissibility of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably you can reformulate your question, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, when you in your statement talk about Jovan Raskovic and his views and influence on Bosanska Krajina, this was an example of the views you were talking about; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I only said that Professor Raskovic was a charismatic personality and he was present when the first boards in Krajina were established. I don't know if he visited later. He wasn't present there much. After the proclamation of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, he didn't go there. He wasn't present all, either physically or politically.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness didn't confirm this aspect of Mr. Raskovic's views, and the Prosecution is trying to basically get admitted that Raskovic thought Dr. Karadzic had a pro-war stance, when the witness didn't confirm or comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did he not confirm to the extent that -- to the extent to agree that Mr. Karadzic's position prevailed at the end of the day?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, his position but not as described by -- he didn't comment on -- on the aspect of his position described in this article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zec, would you like to add --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yeah --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- that was the exact impeachment point, because in the statement it was Mr. Raskovic who gave more foundations or influence in Krajina. And now it contradicts the witness, first; and second, the witness confirmed that this was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Zec. We'll admit this part. Shall we assign a number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6617 [Realtime transcript read in error "P6670"], Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, once the conflict started, the idea of creating Serb areas in Bosnia was implemented by targeting non-Serbs attacking and destroying their towns and places of residence and detaining many. That's what happened; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was there. These things happened very little [Realtime transcript read in error "late"] in Banja Luka. The president of Banja Luka municipality was Mr. Radic, my associate at the institute, and we did our utmost to prevent some uncontrolled groups to do harm to people. I did not witness any of these things and I don't know much about them. However, at the same time, the 14 members of my closest family including my brothers and sisters --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So -- and the fact was that an ethnically clean Serb area was created; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Could we have --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 11, the witness said: Very few of these things happened in Banja Luka, or these things happened very little, not very late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I heard is "very little."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But what is written is "very late."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I confirm that. Yes, shall we continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can we have 65 ter 40606C, which is a video-clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And Mr. Jaksic, you will see a video-clip from a TV talk show where you; Drago Ljubicic from Doboj; and Pero Markovic, from Brcko, talk about the peace plan proposal. There is no date, it could be 1994 or 1995, but perhaps you will be able to tell us the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, transcripts were provided to the translators so they can translate.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "But an even more important point is that really not a single part of Republika Srpska could be found to be returned or to be given to us. I take the expression which would really be a gift to the other side. Not a single area could be found that is not an ethnically clean Serb area. Even if there was no fighting and if so many people did not die for it, to do that would be a sin. But I think that the percentage leads to the following, and I'm warning that that should more or less lead to the following, that's what's being reckoned with, people from Krajina will not given in -- will not give up Krajina. They have an argument. People from Posavina will not give up Posavina. People from Semberija will not give up Semberija. Those in Birac will not give up Birac. Herzegovinians and people from Romanija will not give ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, did you recognise yourself, Drago Ljubicic, and Pero Markovic on this clip?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Of course I recognised myself, and I have almost forgotten these other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us when this was?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I believe that was towards the end of 1994. At that time Republika Srpska had about 72 per cent of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, divisions had already been planned and discussed in percentages, and we were aware that we could not keep 72 per cent of the territory. And there was a lot of talk about where we could make a concession, in which area, and then there occurred a rift between both politicians and regions, each of them calculating which part of which area it could be. And that was the discussion in this show.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And you said: "Not a single area could be found that is not ethnically clean Serb area." At this point in time you were aware of this -- of the results of campaigns to forcibly remove non-Serbs from large areas of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right. I had analyses, and I published them in a book which you have in your possession. The area where Serbs are 92 per cent of the population covers 52 per cent of the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was very difficult, therefore, to find areas where we could make concessions without giving up ethnically pure Serb areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Let's see one more clip from this same discussion with respect to one of these areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That is Pero Markovic discussing the area of Brcko. And we also provided transcript of this clip. It is 65 ter 40406A.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "As for the people who live in Brcko and Posavina, I think the situation is the same. If you remember, Brcko was being divided up to the railroad, up to Brka river, this way, that way. We are sure that Brcko will not and must not be divided, that Brcko will remain Serbian and that it will serve as a connection between Krajinas and motherland Serbia; and that Interplet socks, Bimal oil, Bimeks ham, et cetera, will continue to be sold in Serbian lands. That is to say that we will serve as a connection between Serbian lands in proportion to the future size, and I sincerely hope that they will become as big as we all want them to be."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. Jaksic, Brcko was one of these areas which you refer the ethnically clean areas in Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I found out only after the war, after peace was made. I didn't have any information in Banja Luka concerning Brcko at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender these two clips and I don't have any further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll admit them both.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 40606C will be Exhibit P6618. And 65 ter 40606A will be Exhibit P6619.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, questions were put to you about the union of municipalities. At that time, did we introduce something completely new and violate the law or the constitution by creating this union of municipalities? How did things stand from the legal point of view?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, unions of municipalities existed even before the war. However, they had very little purpose. Certain laws were amended a bit or supplemented to enable life to go on properly. But no new legislation was imposed, especially not laws that would discriminate against certain groups or areas.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P4743. And I ask the witness once again to speak more slowly. P4743. This is the SFRY constitution from 1974. Could we see the Serbian page 22 and 53 in English. Could we zoom in on the lower part of page 119 -- Article 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please, Professor, I'll read out. Everybody can see. It says that communities shall co-operate with one another voluntarily and on principles of solidarity. They shall pull resources and form joint bodies, organisations, and services for the conduct of affairs of common interest and the satisfaction of common needs, and may associate in urban and regional communities. Now, what was going on in Krajina? Was it within the framework of this article?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Precisely. This article was used when this union of municipalities was established because we had no other legal foundation for it. Although we had other areas and other regions, the only legal foundation was this article of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This article straddles the next page, but this was already exhibited as a Prosecution number, so I won't waste time on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I just wanted to note that the English is not a translation of the B/C/S version. This --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The version in B/C/S straddles the next page. Maybe we could see the next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- in the left top corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What I wanted to say is that the B/C/S is the original and the English version is coming from a separate collection. So I noted the distinction between "may" and "shall." I heard the translation "shall," but it is -- it's "may" in English version. I think if we see the cover page, it's a compilation of various constitution of various countries in the world, so I take it it's not the original translation of this original version. With that caveat, we'll continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll have it translated. But "shall" is more appropriate, "shall co-operate voluntarily." And as for association, it says "may associate," or "may join," and "may associate in urban and regional communities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For clarity, I would like to request the CLSS to translate this Article 119.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there is some text on the next page, so the end of this article is on the next page, so I draw your attention to these two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Professor, you have been shown an interview with late Professor Raskovic which is now admitted as P6670.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see that document, please. Prosecution Exhibit 6670.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably 17. We haven't reached that number, 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: 11996, 65 ter that I had.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In line 5 on page 62, it is marked that the exhibit is P6670.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Passage where you are referred to as "pro-war." Yes, 6617.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then on page 62, line 5, it needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in on the middle paragraph; that is to say, the third from the right. One to the left -- right. One more to the left. One more, I'm sorry. Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, here esteemed Prosecutor Zec skipped a passage. It says, "All this may" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably next page for the English, yes. Yes, please, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "All this may sound as some sort of blasphemy but I believe that the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina should not fear Bosnian sovereignty. It would not be genocidal. Perhaps it would not be 'Serbophile,' and it would be 'Serbophobe' but it would not be 'Serbocide." That's what I discussed with Dr. Karadzic. He is not inclined to accept my opinion." Please, Professor, tell us, first of all, were there any indications that that kind of Bosnia would be Serbophobe, and would the Serbian people accept that regardless of what I might have recommended?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: A large part of my statement which I signed and which we discussed is based on the fact that in Krajina there were no rifts between the lines advocated by you on the one hand and Raskovic on the other. After the referendum, it was widely believed that Serbs in Bosnia would not be equal with others. And separation from Yugoslavia was absolutely unacceptable to the population. There was even a conviction that you are even too tolerant and too inclined to believe them more than the people were. I now claim that your position was not hard-line. On the contrary, they were softer and more tolerant concerning the Serbophobia that the people were expecting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the question, line 12, what's missing is the following: Did the policy that was afoot in Bosnia give us reason to view it as Serbophobe, and would people accept it even if I had advised them to accept a unitarian Bosnia? The answer is recorded but I just wanted the question to be complete.

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: The people would not have accepted it even if you had advised them to. The people in Krajina certainly wouldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have further? Shall we continue after a break?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 17 past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.35 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Professor, while we're looking at this document that we have before us, in view of the fact that you were familiar with Yugoslav constitution and laws, were we duty-bound to accept a unilaterally seceding independent BH which would have been Serbophobe as Dr. Raskovic put it?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: I don't think that the constitution of Yugoslavia defined any such scenarios of the breakup of the country unfolding in this way. However, I am quite certain about the fact about the way in which Bosnia-Herzegovina declared its independence was unacceptable to the population in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or shall I say in Krajina. We must be aware of the fact that in Jajce and Bihac, in Krajina therefore, this is where Yugoslavia was born because this is where the thrust of the liberation war took place. The population of the area did not contemplate the idea of leaving Yugoslavia at all. It wasn't necessary to mobilise the population in any way in order to resist this process of declaring Bosnia-Herzegovina independent. And the Serbian people, regardless of whether a referendum would have been held, would never accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And thank you. This is my last question. The TV talk show we were looking at where you talk about the territories being restored within the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, Professor, was it your position and were you saying there that purely Serb territories would have to be restored and in that sense were you talking about the territories that were purely Serb before the war or the territories that we took under our control in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what you meant when you said that territories from Semberija, from here and there, that they would have to be restored and that they would have to be purely Serb?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, there were several plans for the partition of Bosnia, from the Cutileiro Plan, to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, and we were all engaged on the matter. We all contemplated the territories that should fall to us under these plans. Of course, there were quite a few calculating positions that were being planted, bandied about, even within Republika Srpska. So we knew that we would be compelled to give up on some of the territories in order to end up with compact territory. In that context, we were apprehensive of the fact, and this is something that turned out to be true under the Dayton Accords, we were apprehensive of the fact that we would have to give up on purely Serb territories. It was never our position that we should count on the territories that were conquered in any way. Ultimately, it had to do with part of the Herzegovina, western Bosnia, Drvar, Glamoc. All these territories ultimately ended up in the federation. What we had in mind were the territories where over 90 per cent of the population was Serbs and they were the periphery of what was the then layout of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When we say "purely Serb," this means "indubitably Serb." Was Banja Luka purely Serb during the war?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Not during the war it wasn't. The records reflecting the various percentages was not something that we were able to have. In my institute, people kept on working until 1994. However, there were waves of people moving out in the outlying areas, and this led to a psychosis where people grouped, where people left. But never during the war did we contemplate this, and the majority of us were in fact afraid of being ethnically pure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you say you didn't contemplate this, you didn't treat them, who is "we," and how were the Muslims leaving Banja Luka treated? Were they driven out?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that there were people who left the institute and they were weeping. We didn't sack them. They simply left of their own accord. Were they organised by someone? Did they have to leave? I don't know. But I know quite a few people. I know people who came to see me at home who told me, I don't have the intention of leaving but a group was getting organised and advising me to join them and pack up our things. So many people were involved and we weren't quite clear on what the motivations were. Perhaps there was pressure exerted on some, but in many cases I think it was the case of departures that were organised and prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And who initiated these departures? Was it the authorities or they themselves?

utterances.speaker: DUSKO JAKSIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that. Not the local authorities, no. President Radic, in fact, was confronted with a great deal of problems. He was often said to be the man who failed to respond to allegations that Serbs in some other areas were being driven out, and he was often reproached for being too tolerant. Our view was that we should not give into such statements and that we should not facilitate or in any way assist this process of people moving out of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then that concludes your evidence, Mr. Jaksic. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So next witness is Mr. Jovo Kevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would the witness make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kevac. Please be seated and make yourself comfortable. Yes. Before you commence your evidence, Mr. Kevac, I must draw your attention to a certain rule that we have here at this international Tribunal; that is, Rule 90(E). Under this rule, you may object to answering any question from Mr. Karadzic, the Prosecutor, or even from the Judges if you believe that your answer might incriminate you in a criminal offence. In this context, "incriminate" means saying something that might amount to an admission of your guilt in a criminal offence, or saying something that might provide evidence that you might have committed a criminal offence. However, should you think that an answer might incriminate you and as a consequence you refuse to answer the question, I must let you know that the Tribunal has the power to compel you to answer the question. But in that situation, the Tribunal would ensure that your testimony compelled under such circumstances would not be used in any case that might be laid against you for any offence save and except the offence of giving false testimony. Do you understand that, Mr. Kevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was a bit too fast. Please let's make a pause and make sure that we speak slowly so that everything may be reflected in the transcript without resorting to the need to repeat things. Mr. Kevac, have you given a statement to my Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May the witness be shown 1D49065.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting, Jovo is short for Jovan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please look at the left-hand side. Is this the first page of your statement?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you read the statement and signed it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the last page be shown so that the witness may identify the signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the statement accurately reflect what you told the Defence team?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to put the same questions to you here today in the courtroom, would your answers essentially be the same?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender this statement into evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Edgerton. Do you have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will now read a short summary of the statement in English, the statement by Mr. Jovo Kevac. [In English] Jovo Kevac was elected to the Kljuc Municipal Assembly in 1990. In 1992, he was mobilised in the JNA and assigned to the war unit 820, the Banja Luka training centre. The Kljuc Municipal Assembly had an absolute majority of SDS members. The assembly continued to operate normally until the events in Croatia and Slovenia, after which concern spread among all citizens. When the first incident occurred, the Muslim leaders had already formed their own Stari Grad municipality and their own BH Territorial Defence. A particularly serious incident occurred when Muslim extremists set up an ambush on the road between Velagici and Pudin Han and attacked a column of young, unarmed soldiers on regular military service in the JNA. On this occasion, six soldiers were killed and about twenty wounded. As it became clear from numerous attacks, the Muslim extremists were preparing for war with the Serbs in Kljuc. This is also confirmed by the fact that the Muslims moved a large number of Muslim civilians from the area of Velagici along to Slovenia, Croatia, and other European countries before the first incident. During and after these events, the situation was chaotic: Roads and telecommunications were cut, there were disruptions to the water-supply, shortage of medicine, food, and fuel, and there was no electricity. The safety of every citizen was compromised regardless of affiliation or ethnicity, since individuals and groups were roaming around and seeking personal and financial benefits. The chaos in Kljuc lasted until the establishment of political authorities and of VRS and civilian police. They immediately ordered that a system be created to ensure the safety and protection of all citizens of Kljuc and the political leadership offered co-existence to everyone. Many Muslims remained in Kljuc in 1992-1993 and some joined the civilian structures. After the first incident in Kljuc municipality, panic and chaos took hold and all those who had relatives or friends somewhere abroad tried to leave. It was not only Muslims and Croats who did so, but also Serbs. The SDS and the military authorities of Kljuc municipality never planned or ordered the ethnic cleansing of the municipality. All citizens who did not participate in combat operations and attacks on Serbs were allowed to stay. On 28th of May, 1992, the leadership of Kljuc municipality appealed to everyone in possession of illegal weapons to hand them over to the legal organs of the civilian police in order to avoid untoward incidents. The Muslims who did not want to hand in their weapons ran away and tried to join the Muslim forces on the territory outside Kljuc. After the ultimatum, those who were found in possession of illegal arms were taken to the Secretariat of the Interior, SUP, office to be interrogated. Mr. Kevac is not aware of any beating that occurred during and outside these investigations. On 10th of July, 1992, Bosnian Muslim men and women were killed at the school building of the Biljani hamlet. This heinous crime was committed by individuals who got out of control. They were arrested and handed over to the prosecution authorities in Banja Luka. And that is summary. At that moment, I do not have questions for Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Kevac, as you have noted, your evidence in chief in this case has been admitted in writing; that is, through your written witness statement in lieu of your oral testimony. Now, you'll be cross-examined by the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like to begin your cross-examination by going straight to a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's 65 ter number 09225, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right. This document, Mr. Kevac, is a report dated July 13, 1992, from the security organ of the 30th Krajina Division, and, Mr. Kevac, it's responding to a Main Staff query dated the same day, and the query was about paramilitary and other units in the division's area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'd like us to go over in both languages to page 3, please, in English and in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kevac, have a look at that paragraph that's at the top of the page in your language, while we'll have a look at the same paragraph that's in the middle of the page in English. And it says: "The revival of the Chetnik movement is present in the area of the Kljuc municipality and the promoters there are the SDS President Veljko Kondic, a close relative of Vinko Kondic, from the Kljuc SSJB 'Vojvoda' Jovo Kevac, reserve captain 1st class, is a member of the units formed on that territory. In the end of April, Kevac provoked a rebellion in the education centre of Stricici and prevented the sending of 117 scripts and officers to a war unit of the 1st Krajina Corps. On his return to the territory of Kljuc, the political leadership appointed him a company commander and later on he was transferred to the position of battalion commander in that area." That's you; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And whatever this document says, you were integrated into the VRS; right? You were -- not only as a company commander, a battalion commander, but for a period of time you even served as a brigade commander in the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: I was not a brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. But in terms of your positions and ranks, the document's correct. You were a company commander and you were a battalion commander; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: I was a -- I was the commander of a company as it was being set up, and likewise the battalion commander. It was only at the end of August that the battalion was in fact formed and that I was appointed its commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. Now your statement doesn't say a word about any of that; right? It doesn't have a word about your military service. All it says is that -- in fact, if I hadn't have asked you anything else, we would all have understood that you spent your service in the training centre in Banja Luka, because that's all your statement says; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: I did say that we returned to the municipality as the 820th Training Centre was disbanded. As an experienced officer, with previous experience of work at the TO Staff, at this point in time when it was not possible to gain access to the records of conscripts, I was taken on because of my experience to gather the units that would come under the 17th Kljuc Brigade. And that's why, as you say, I was company commander and battalion commander. I didn't think it necessary to describe my entire warpath. But if necessary, I can describe for you the various places where I was deployed to during the war and the posts I was appointed to.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to that. But, Mr. Kevac, your statement doesn't even say that you returned to the municipality as the 820th Training Center was disbanded. It says absolutely nothing about your military service record; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry if that's the way it is, but right now I cannot remember what it was that I wrote. But I believe that that was so. However, not with the intention of avoiding anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, you say now that you omitted that significant period of time of service, not with the intention of avoiding anything, but, Mr. Kevac, that period of service -- in that period of service, you were a member and you were a commander of units who were involved in crimes against non-Serbs in Prhovo, in Peci, in Velagici, and Biljani. Mr. Kevac, what I'd like to put to you is that you deliberately -- you deliberately hid your military service record because you had a personal interest in doing so. You wanted to avoid criminal investigation. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: No, no, Madam Prosecutor, that is not the case. No intention whatsoever. And all the things that you enumerated, namely, that the non-Serb population was killed at these locations, that is not correct. The only thing that may have happened was the village of Biljani, where I tried, as briefly as possible, to explain how come that happened. As for all the rest that you enumerated previously, I was not there at all, and that was not something that my unit did and it was not their line of work, either.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kevac, your fellow soldiers, including Marko Adamovic, and your company commander, your subordinate company commander, Marko Samardzija, have both been convicted of crimes arising from the actions of your military forces at these locations, Marko Samardzija, in particular, for his in the events at Biljani on the 10th of July. So, Mr. Kevac, it's not the truth that guided you in making this statement. As I said, it was your direct personal interest in avoiding investigation, isn't it? Otherwise, without my questioning right now we would never have known what you were doing; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: First of all, I would kindly ask you not to use that expression, that I am saying something that is not true. I am telling the truth. Marko Adamovic and the units that you enumerated were never subordinated to me. Marko Adamovic was subordinated to me at the Territorial Defence Staff in peacetime. He was one of my desk officers. In wartime, no. Marko Samardzija was also a company commander, a commander of a company that was being established because he hailed from that village. If you allow me, I can give an explanation. The unit was not in barracks. The units were at home. I mean, the personnel, the members of these units. There were lists that we managed to complete. Marko worked on the establishment of that unit, and after that he was not commander of that unit. So there is no wish or intention on our part to conceal anything here. But, please, I kindly ask you, if possible, to refrain from saying that I am not telling the truth. Rest assured that I am telling the truth, and it is my wish to clarify all of these matters, as a matter of fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you're telling the truth now, but you were hiding the truth when you signed that statement. That's what you're telling us.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Oh, please. Why did you not put a question to me in terms of speaking about my statement. I thought that this was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness repeat his second sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had you put the questions that you were supposed to put to me, believe me, I would have provided an extensive answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, the interpreters are concerned that they might have missed your second sentence or your sentence after you responded: "Why did you not put a question to me in terms of speaking about my statement." What did you say after that? What we have here is that you said that you thought that this was sufficient. Do you confirm that's what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I thought that that was sufficient. But before that, I also said that I would have given an extensive explanation about my movements. I thought that was the question. I thought that that was sufficient. I made myself available.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's have a look --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Before I move on, could I have the first document, 65 ter number 09225, tendered as a Prosecution exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6620, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Let's go on to another document.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's P3366, please. I just need to check that I have the right 65 ter number. That's good. We have the correct documents in front of us now.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Have a look at this one, Mr. Kevac. This is an Official Note dated July 10, 1992, and it's prepared by the commander of the Sanica public security station. And it's about the moping up in Sanica by the military organs or the battalion of Commander Jovo Kevac. That's you again; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: That is me, but I repeat to you yet again that in that period I was not commander. Rather, I was carrying out the replenishment of the battalion and training the commander of that battalion. I became commander of that battalion on the basis of an official order in the month of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Regardless of whatever title you're now saying that you might have held at the time of the action in Biljani, it's clear that this document is referring to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This document says that the commander of the police station in Sanica was informed by you that the next day your units would undertake a moping-up operation in the terrain in Biljani. It says that the job of the police was to take over the military prisoners, to put them in the school in Biljani, and that they got help from the mobile intervention unit of the Kljuc SJB. It says that the action at Biljani happened in constant communication with the military and that it was the military who sent two buses from Kljuc to take the prisoners there. So this document says you were the commander of a co-ordinated operation that ended with the killing of more than 100 unarmed men, Mr. Kevac. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: These words of yours really give rise to something that I have to put this way: This term, "moping up the terrain," or rather, "cleansing the terrain," is not used in military terminology. It was mostly used by policemen believing that that is a search of the wider area. In this case --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, Mr. Kevac, I didn't ask you about that. My question was that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I think he was being responsive to her question. She should give him a chance to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am not sure he was answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Excellency. I think that the Prosecution's question suggested cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll hear him from the meaning of "moping up" and then proceed. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you addressing me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I repeat once again: "Ciscenje terena" is not military terminology. It was used in the police. I meant searching the broader area. Now, why did this commander use that term? I don't know. Probably because in their own communications they use the term several times because this term was used in peacetime as well. The task of this unit, as mentioned here, was to have the Muslim population, the men, gathered in a single place and this was being said to people from one home to another. Members of the unit went around saying that. But then these people were at their homes all the time. They were carrying out their regular duties, standing guard duty at night and also they had reinforced patrols. So this unit was involved in the following way: These men were brought together and the security services, military and civilian, were supposed to deal with persons who were of security interest. Now an explanation: Persons who did not hand over illegal weapons, persons who were marked as incident prone, and also when that would be completed people would go home, except for those persons who were supposed to be investigated. This was not a single case only. It would also happen in the territory of the municipality where there were absolutely no incidents whatsoever. Persons of security interest would be singled out and the rest would be sent to their homes. Now, why did this happen? We'll probably discuss that a bit more. I kindly ask you, though, to understand, to the extent you can for the sake of the truth, what the times were like and what the conditions were like.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I may, I'd like to get back to my question. My question was about what this document says. My question was: This document says that you were the commander of a co-ordinated operation that ended with the killing of more than 100 men. You were the commander; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: I repeat for the third time: No, I was not commander. Another explanation, now. As for the relationship with the civilian authorities, that is to say, this military unit with the civilian authorities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- this was dealt with by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The question has nothing to do with the co-operation with the police. Wait for the next question. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So are you saying that this document which says on its face -- which refers on its face to you about the moping-up action in Sanica by military organs or the battalion of the commander Jovan Kevac is wrong? You were the 2nd Battalion commander, weren't you? You were in charge.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Let's deal with it this way. This document is written in a grotesque way. I am saying this in linguistic and logical terms. I am stating to you for sure that I was not the responsible person and that I was not the commander of the unit at the time. Quite simply, I was an officer whose task was to establish the battalion in these impossible conditions, if I can put it that way, and to train the command that had been manned with inappropriate military specialties. So that's it. I really don't see what it is that you want me to add to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you completely hid your military service record from all of us in the first place. And now that I confront you with it and now that I confront you with a document that puts you in command of an operation that resulted in the killing of more than a hundred men, you say the document is wrong, that it's a lie. You're just trying to avoid investigation, Mr. Kevac. That's why you didn't tell us about it in the first place; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: You're going back to my answer to the question that I have already answered. I have no reason to hide my movements during the war, but these insinuations, these things that you are trying to pin on me, that cannot relate to this. And I repeat to you once again: This is not a wrongful report. This is a grotesque report. That's a difference that can be stated in our language. Or how do I clarify this? It's just clumsy. It's worded in a clumsy way without any kind of ill intentions. Now, why would one not believe me? After all, I took an oath a moment ago stating that I would tell the truth, and this is the truth, 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Well, let's go to the evidence of somebody else who took an oath in front of another Chamber of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: 65 ter number 25953.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And it's the evidence of a witness who testified in the prosecution of General Mladic. Her name was Ms. Birte Weiss, and she's an experienced journalist with more than 25 years of service in the Danish cabinet who went back to journalism. And she testified in front of the Judges in the trial of General Mladic about her conversations with Marko Samardzija in relation to the killings at Biljani on the 10th of July, 1992. And you see the page in front of you of her testimony. And she wrote a book that talked about the events in Kljuc and Biljani, and she said in respect of the events of 10 July 1992 Samardzija told her that he called the Commander-in-Chief and told him what was about to happen in Biljani. Shove off. Go home, he just said. That was at 9.00 a.m. and there were as yet no dead on the road, all those terrible things that he first heard about later. And then I don't know if the second page of this has been uploaded, so I'll just read it otherwise. And then Mrs. Weiss was asked: "Did Marko Samardzija tell you who he called? Did he specifically give the name of who he called?" And she answered: "He mentioned that he contacted the people he could get in touch with. He created the impression that he -- both on the spot, that he objected on the spot, and he mentioned the name Jovo Kevac. And in addition, by telephone he contacted several people whom he wanted to tell what was going on in Biljani in those hours." And then she was asked again -- and I'm reading this to you in case you don't understand English. She was asked again: "And did he tell you who those several people were or what office they occupied?" And she answered: "He said that they were the commanding people." So you told us that you weren't the responsible person but Mrs. Weiss told us that Samardzija said that's exactly who you were. You were one of the commanders, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And that's, for the record, Mladic transcript pages 5303 to 5304.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kevac, I'll show you something else and then I'll ask you a question. She's not the only one. In his own trial in front of the state court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Samardzija gave evidence. And he was convicted on appeal to custodial time for the crimes -- for crimes relating to the events in Biljani.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: If we could have a look at 65 ter number 25898, just in case you want to see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But I can read it to you as well. That's a copy of the appellate decision in the case of --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be possible -- would it be possible to have shorter questions? Please, I'm afraid that we're going to turn the questions into a salad, and then the answers are going to be inadequate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's up to the Chamber. The Chamber will monitor the appropriateness of questions. Please continue, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: At page 30 of this decision, and I'm going to see if I can try quickly to find the B/C/S citation, I might have omitted to do it, but, in any case, it's English page 30. The appellate court referred to Samardzija's evidence in his own Defence, and Samardzija said at Biljani, seeing the civilians loaded on the buses, he contacted you and told you something strange was happening. He told you he needed further instructions. He referred to you by name. My question to you is: Given this evidence --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that part at least be shown to the witness in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I can do it in a few minutes, Dr. Karadzic, and -- because I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, it's important to show it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I accept that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could I have your indulgence, then, for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Because I didn't bring a B/C/S hard copy with me, so it will take me a couple of minutes. And my apologies. Your Honour, my sincere apologies at this. Would Your Honours indulge me with a few short minutes of recess rather than wasting anyone's time? And it would be very brief for us to find this -- oh, my colleagues in the Registry who are able to read the language have been able to save the day, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Kevac, the citation I was referring to is in the first full paragraph, the large portion, the large full paragraph at the top of the page in front of you about halfway through that paragraph. And the exact citation says: "The testimony of the witnesses Slavko Strbac and Drago Banjac confirms the defence of the accused that he made a contact with his superior Jovo Kevac, the brigade commander, and that on that occasion he said something strange was happening and that he needed further instructions."

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And my thanks to my colleagues, my sincere thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, what I'd like to put to you is: You were in charge. You knew about the crimes. You knew about them at the time they were happening. You're only -- what you're doing, actually, is only trying to create doubt now about this incident because it's in your personal interest to do so. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: No. And, please, with these questions that are finally to your benefit, you are not maintaining the dignity of the Prosecution. The answer to this question is no. And I will give an explanation to each and every question, if it is the right question, but I really do not appreciate these insinuations.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just to stay --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the reference to Jovan Kavac in this document, does it refer to you, Mr. Kevac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because Jovo and Jovan is approximately the same in our language. It's very common.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But it says "Kavac" not "Kevac." It's a misspelling. It's a typo.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a typo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So despite what Mr. Samardzija said under oath in his own trial, despite what Ms. Weiss said under oath before this Tribunal, you maintain that you were not the responsible person in respect of the events in Biljani; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But you are not letting me explain how that communication went. It would be clearer to both you and the Court. The communications were down in the entire territory of Kljuc. The only connection --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: -- that existed with the local commune Sanica was through radio sets that had a limited range, and then an interim radio station had to be established. One of these interim stations was at the top of a hill called Biljani. All communications were by radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac --

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: The first contact with Samardzija --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's just let him --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's just hear him out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first communication between this radio was between Marko Samardzija and assistant commander for legal, moral guidance, and legal affairs. The assignment of the unit of which Marko Samardzija was a member was, after gathering Muslim men and after the security people arrived, to let them go home. I repeated that to Marko, as far as I remember. So there was no contact in which I was asked what to do because that had already been communicated to these people. And there is no reason for this kind of communication not to be understood as it really went because the entire civilian and military life operated through these three radio stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, I have a request that the remainder of the cross-examination on this subject be heard in closed session, and the reason for that request is that the last time we had a witness from Kljuc that Ms. Edgerton cross-examined and put to that witness that he was responsible for crimes in Biljani and other areas of Kljuc was Marko Adamovic, who at the time he testified, had been acquitted of those crimes. Two weeks after his testimony, his conviction was -- his acquittal was overturned and he was convicted and sentenced to prison, and it remains unclear to what extent the public broadcast of his testimony had any influence on that, and I think it's in the interest of the witness if she's going to be putting this kind of cross-examination to him, and then looking through the exhibits that they have notified us, it seems like that's the direction in which it's going, I think it's in the interest of this witness that the testimony be in closed session so that he doesn't suffer the same fate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So your basis again? The witness is not invoking his right to refuse to testify about incriminating events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct and we appreciate that. But given the fact that these events are the subject of prosecution in the court of Bosnia, it appears that it's in the best interest of the witness and the Chamber that the testimony of this nature be given in closed session. And I note that the witness also doesn't have counsel, so he doesn't have anyone to raise that issue other than me doing it for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that's something Mr. Tieger will address you on, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is inappropriate of Mr. Robinson to raise this entirely speculative and unfounded assertion about the alleged relationship between a -- an ongoing legal proceeding and our trial here. He has no basis whatsoever for making this claim except the thinnest of insinuations. He's the one who has been pressing at every possible juncture for an open trial. Even if there was some basis for doing that, the -- going into closed session or private session could only have the opposite impact in that it would have a -- the strongest of suggestions that the events about which this witness is explaining and protesting his innocence were highly incriminatory to the witness because we went into the private session when it would seem to me would stimulate investigations in prosecutions rather than anything else. In any event, particularly given the standard raised by the Defence during the course of this proceeding, there seems to be no basis whatsoever for taking the action suggested by Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber agrees with Mr. Tieger. And the witness hasn't invoked his right pursuant to Rule 90(E) not to answer the questions which would incriminate him. And further, all Ms. Edgerton has done was put questions based upon the documents which are publicly available, including the judgement. So the Chamber is not satisfied the Chamber should go into private session. Mr. Kevac, I take it you understand what we just discussed. But I just wanted to remind you that you have a right not to answer the question or notwithstanding the fact that the Chamber still has the power to compel you to answer the question, as I advised you at the outset of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for this. But I reckoned and I still reckon on speaking the truth and only the truth. But in giving my answers, I was focused only on the answers and forgot about that right. I thank Mr. Robinson. But indeed, if we want to find as much truth as possible and as much as I know, then it would be a good idea to apply these other measures as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you in full. Could you be more specific, Mr. Kevac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My wish is to tell the real truth to the extent that I know. And in focusing on answers and events, I had forgotten about invoking that right, and I thank Mr. Robinson for reminding me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll proceed and see how it evolves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think he's asking -- maybe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- we're not understanding it the same way but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you may invoke your privilege not to answer the question which -- the answer of which may incriminate you in a criminal offence depending upon the question. So we'll hear the question from Ms. Edgerton and see whether you trigger that privilege or not. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, given that we have come to the end of our court day, I would ask that the Trial Chamber take a recess at this time and give Mr. Kevac the opportunity to consult with a counsel to be assigned to him so that he could understand what his rights are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. Who is going to assign counsel to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I am asking the Chamber to have Registry provide him with an assigned counsel so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The basis of which is what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The basis of which is that he now has expressed an indication to possibly take advantage of protective -- of measures that could protect his rights for self-incrimination. Those could include asserting his right not to answer a question or requesting a closed session. And I'm not the --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not his lawyer, so that --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: -- isn't this a discussion that is better had in the absence of the witness? I'm sorry, I don't mean anything inappropriate, but just a note of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember the Chamber once referred to the three categories of persons to whom the Tribunal will assign counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President. And I also remember your ruling in the case of Mr. Kovac, that when there are exceptional circumstances, the Chamber would assign counsel to someone even if they don't fit within those tree categories. And I think that this comes within that, because we have now -- if you look at the exhibits that the Prosecution is proposing to use, I think you'll understand even better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber clearly advised him of his right before he commenced giving his testimony, and I repeated it now. And therefore the Chamber sees no basis to suspend the proceeding at the moment. We continue. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just ask one thing. The witness said that perhaps it would not be a bad idea to think of other measures --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like the Chamber to find out whether that meant closing the session. Did he mean closing the session? The witness has the right to ask for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber was not satisfied to go into private session at the time. We'll see, and then depending upon the question, if the witness invokes his right pursuant to Rule 90(E), the Chamber consider his request again. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mr. Kevac, I'd just like to go back some time in the discussion to the last answer that you gave, to remind you of it, and I'd like to ask you a question based on that. You said the first communication between this radio was between Marko Samardzija and the assistant commander for legal and morale guidance and legal affairs. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: That was Spasoje Djukanovic. Late Spasoje Djukanovic, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. You then said that: "The assignment of the unit of which Marko Samardzija was a member, after gathering Muslim men and after security people arrived, was to let them go home. I repeated that to Marko, as far as I remember." So my question to you is based on that answer. You would agree that you were the superior officer of Marko Samardzija; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: I don't know which answer to give you to explain I was not. And how am I supposed to explain my role in that case and in that unit up to August? If it can be of any assistance. I refused to be the commander of that unit for my personal reasons, and some of the suspicions I had at the time unfortunately came true. However, when it came to the moment when the unit was supposed to go into combat, a Serbian officer does not decline to serve because among other virtues he has the virtue of valour and honour, and that is why then I accepted to be the commander. All the way up to then, I was just the commanding officer engaged in completely different assignments, mainly to do with the establishment and training of the unit. The command of the unit had two levels: Group occupations and staff combat drills. Because people who occupied those positions in the command never actually did these things. I, on the other hand, had knowledge about All People's Defence and the regulations enabled me to do this. So my job was to establish the battalion and train the battalion. And in communication, some other terms were perhaps sometimes used.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in regard -- looking at the answer you just gave, I'd like to ask you this: In regard to this operation, do I understand you to say that you accepted to be the commander? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: I accepted the duty of commander in August, and this is July. In the end of August, I received the order appointing me.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now going back to this same answer that I had just read out to you in part, am I correct in understanding that at that day - 10 July 1992 - you did have communication with Marko Samardzija?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yeah. I want you to confirm what you said. You said -- I'll read you the sentence. You said: "The assignment of the unit of which Marko Samardzija was a member, after gathering Muslim men and after the security people arrived, was to let them go home. I repeated that to Marko, as far as I can remember." That means you did have communication with Marko Samardzija on the 10th of July, 1992, at Biljani. That's what your answer means; right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to emphasise once again because it will make it easier for both you and me. The assignment, when I said to let them go home, I meant that the members of that unit should go home after finishing their assignment because there was no other assignment. And my communication with Marko was the second communication, because the first communication he had was with the assistant commander for morale guidance, legal, and religious affairs. I was not there at the moment he called -- they called me, and I repeated what was said to them before: When you finish this, go home. Because I explained to you before, these people were not in the barracks. They were in their own homes. They guarded their own villages, standing guard and doing patrol, and we had a list of them as members of the battalion. And I've told you the same thing in my previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So Marko called you, contacted you, told you something strange was happening, and your evidence is: Send the men home. Right?

utterances.speaker: JOVO KEVAC
utterances.text: That's only one talk. I would remember. Marko never told me that. He never even confirmed it when he came to the station when I saw him. He didn't say anything was afoot. And finally, I couldn't even know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see there is about, by my computer, one minute to go in the court day and probably to get the next sentence out would take me more than that one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll adjourn here today. Mr. Kevac, we'll continue tomorrow morning at 9.00. Can I advise you not to discuss with anybody else about your testimony while you are giving evidence here. But it does not prohibit you from getting opinion, consultation from any lawyer if you so wish. But, Mr. Robinson, the Chamber finds no basis to assign counsel for the witness at the moment. The case of Mr. Tomo Kovac was different and not comparable to this witness. He was once interviewed as a suspect by the Prosecutor and with counsel assigned, and in another proceeding he was already assigned counsel. So that was the basis on which we allowed counsel to be assigned to Tomo Kovac. Hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 30th day of January, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.47 p.m.,
